blocks.text: The intravenous (IV) giving set is a sterile disposable device used to deliver fluids, medications, blood-compatible solutions, or other prescribed intravenous preparations from a container into a patient's venous circulation.
In an OSCE, you may be asked to identify the device, name its parts, demonstrate how to prime it, calculate an infusion rate, or identify errors that could compromise patient safety.
Name: Intravenous giving set (IV infusion set).
Classification: Sterile, single-use medical device for intravenous fluid administration.
Other names: IV administration set, infusion giving set, IV tubing.
Principle: Gravity-driven infusion or delivery through a compatible infusion pump.
Two common types are:
Delivers relatively large drops, commonly 10, 15 or 20 drops/mL, depending on the manufacturer's specification.
Usually delivers 60 drops/mL. Useful when accurate, low-volume gravity infusion is needed.
Important: Always read the drop factor printed on the packaging. Do not assume that every macrodrip set has the same calibration.
An IV giving set is used when a patient requires a prescribed substance to be administered directly into a vein.
Common indications include:
Fluid replacement: e.g., isotonic crystalloids for appropriate dehydration or hypovolaemia.
Maintenance fluids: when oral or enteral intake is inadequate and IV maintenance is indicated.
Medication administration: compatible IV medications diluted and prescribed for infusion.
Electrolyte replacement: prescribed solutions such as potassium-containing fluids, with appropriate concentration and rate controls.
Perioperative care: delivery of prescribed fluids during and after surgery.
Emergency treatment: controlled administration of appropriate IV fluids during resuscitation.
Blood component administration: only when a suitable, approved blood transfusion set is used.

OSCE distinction: An ordinary IV giving set is not automatically suitable for blood transfusion, lipid-containing preparations, or every medication. The required tubing and filter depend on the product and institutional protocol.
Pierces the designated port of the IV fluid container and connects the giving set to it. It must remain sterile.
Allows visual observation and counting of drops. It is partially filled during priming.
Compresses the tubing to regulate or stop gravity-driven flow. It does not reliably control the rate of a pressurised or pump-driven infusion by itself.
Carries fluid from the container towards the patient's vascular access. It must be free of kinks, leaks and air before connection.

blocks.text: Provides access for compatible medication administration using the correct aseptic technique. Not all sets contain one.
Connects the giving set to a compatible IV cannula or extension set, often through a Luer-lock connection.
Other possible features include an air vent for certain rigid containers, a back-check valve, a filter or a protective cap. These are design-dependent.
Provides direct access to the systemic circulation.
Allows prescribed fluids and compatible medications to be administered continuously.
Gravity infusion can work without electrical power.
Drop rate can be adjusted using a roller clamp.
Compatible sets can connect to infusion pumps for more controlled delivery.
The drip chamber allows visual monitoring of flow.
Disposable sterile sets reduce contamination risk when used correctly.
Incorrect rates can cause fluid overload, under-infusion or medication toxicity.
Gravity infusion rates can change with the height of the fluid container, patient position, venous pressure and tubing resistance.
Air in the line can create a risk of air embolism, particularly in susceptible circumstances.
Connections may leak, disconnect or become contaminated.
Tubing can kink or become obstructed.
The set does not confirm that the cannula is correctly positioned or that fluid is entering the vein.
Gravity infusion is less precise than a properly configured infusion pump for many medications and small-volume infusions.
Before demonstrating the procedure, state that you would:
Perform hand hygiene.
Confirm the prescription, patient identity, fluid type, volume, route and intended rate.
Check allergies and any relevant fluid restrictions.
Inspect the fluid container for expiry, leaks, damaged packaging, discolouration or particles.
Check that the giving set is sterile, intact, within expiry and appropriate for the intended fluid.
Explain the procedure to the patient and obtain consent.
Prepare a clean working area and use aseptic non-touch technique.
Check the IV cannula site for pain, swelling, redness, leakage or other signs of complications.
Ensure the clamp is closed before inserting the spike into the fluid container.
Confirm that the tubing and connector are compatible with the intended device and solution.
Examiner's tip: Never touch the sterile spike, the exposed sterile connector or other critical sterile surfaces.

subsections.subsection_title: How to use an IV giving set — step-by-step OSCE demonstration

blocks.text: Gather the prescribed IV fluid, sterile giving set, appropriate IV access, antiseptic supplies and any required infusion device. Perform hand hygiene and verify the prescription.
Ensure the clamp is fully closed before connecting the set to the fluid container to prevent uncontrolled flow.
Remove the protective covers as directed by the manufacturer. Insert the spike into the designated port using aseptic technique without touching critical surfaces.
Squeeze the chamber gently until it reaches the manufacturer's recommended fill level, commonly around one-third to one-half full.

Open the clamp and allow the prescribed fluid to flow through the tubing until it is completely filled and air is expelled. Keep the distal connector sterile and do not allow fluid to splash or contaminate it.
Examine the tubing for air bubbles, kinks, leaks and damaged connections. Ensure the distal end remains sterile. Never connect an unprimed line to a patient.
Assess the cannula site, disinfect the needleless connector as required and allow it to dry. Connect the primed set aseptically using a compatible connector.

items: Step 8 — Set and verify the rate

blocks.text: Set the prescribed rate using the appropriate pump or, for gravity infusion, the roller clamp and calculated drop rate. Check that the fluid is flowing appropriately.

Check the patient, infusion rate, tubing, connections and cannula site. Document the fluid, start time, prescribed rate and relevant observations. Reassess according to the patient's condition and local protocol.

“I would verify the prescription and patient identity, maintain aseptic technique, close the clamp, connect the sterile giving set, partially fill the drip chamber and prime the tubing completely. I would then assess the IV site, connect the set aseptically, establish the prescribed rate and monitor the patient for infiltration, phlebitis, fluid overload and other complications.”
Clinical safety: In an actual clinical setting, follow local policy and manufacturer instructions. Some infusions require specific tubing, filters, pump settings or additional checks.
An IV giving set has no universal absolute contraindication in isolation. Its use depends on the prescribed therapy, the patient's vascular access and the suitability of the device.

Air in the line is a preventable hazard; clinically significant air embolism is uncommon with routine peripheral infusions but can be serious
Under-delivery, overdose or rapid fluid administration
Fluid loss, contamination and interruption of therapy

blocks.text: If a complication is suspected: Stop or pause the infusion as clinically appropriate, assess the patient and IV site, and escalate promptly. For suspected extravasation, follow the specific drug protocol; do not automatically flush the line or remove the cannula before following the recommended management steps.
The giving set itself does not produce diagnostic findings, but the examiner may expect you to assess whether the infusion is functioning correctly.
Tubing is primed and free of visible air.
Connections are secure, with no leaks.
Fluid is running at the prescribed rate.
Cannula site is comfortable, without swelling or redness.
Patient is tolerating the infusion.
Infusion is too fast, too slow or has stopped unexpectedly.
Air bubbles, kinks, disconnections or leaks are present.
There is pain, swelling, redness or leakage at the cannula site.
The patient develops breathlessness, deterioration or other signs of intolerance.
This is a particularly important section for a Medicine and Pediatrics OSCE.
Weight-based fluid calculations: Prescribe and calculate fluids according to the child's weight, age, clinical condition and applicable protocol.
Fluid overload: Infants and children can deteriorate if excessive fluid is administered. Monitor intake, output, weight and clinical status as indicated.
Microdrip sets: A 60-drop/mL set can be useful for low-rate gravity infusions, but it does not replace an infusion pump when precise delivery is required.
Infusion pumps: Prefer appropriately configured, validated pumps for small volumes and medications requiring accurate rates, especially in neonates.
Cannula security: Secure the cannula and tubing to reduce accidental displacement, while keeping the insertion site visible for inspection.
Caregiver involvement: Explain the procedure to the child and caregiver in age-appropriate language.
Neonatal caution: Very small fluid volumes, narrow safety margins and rapid clinical changes make accurate prescribing and close monitoring essential.
Medication safety: Never estimate a child's medication dose from age alone when a weight-based or other specific dosing protocol is required.

High-yield point: A microdrip set delivers 60 drops/mL, so under gravity infusion, 60 drops per minute corresponds numerically to 60 mL/hour. However, this relationship assumes the specified drop factor and a stable gravity flow.

subsections.subsection_title: Common OSCE questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is an IV giving set?
It is a sterile disposable device that carries prescribed IV fluids or compatible preparations from a container into a patient's venous circulation.
Q2. What is the function of the drip chamber?
It allows visual observation and counting of drops and helps prevent air from entering the tubing during appropriate setup.
Q3. Differentiate macrodrip and microdrip sets.
Macrodrip sets have larger drops and commonly have calibration factors of 10, 15 or 20 drops/mL. Microdrip sets typically deliver 60 drops/mL and are useful for low-rate gravity infusions.
Q4. Why must the tubing be primed?
To fill the tubing with fluid and expel air before connecting it to the patient, reducing the risk of air entry and ensuring the line is ready for use.
Q5. Can you use a standard IV giving set for a blood transfusion?
Not automatically. Use a designated, approved blood administration set with the appropriate filter and follow the transfusion protocol.
Q6. What would you do if the infusion stops flowing?

Assess the patient and inspect the tubing, clamp, connections and cannula site for kinks, obstruction, displacement or infiltration. Correct only what is safe and within my scope, and escalate if the cause is unclear. Never force fluid through a suspected obstruction.
Q7. What is the drop factor?
It is the number of drops delivered per millilitre by a specific giving set, as stated by the manufacturer.
Q8. Why might an infusion run faster than expected?

The fluid container may be positioned too high, the clamp may be too open, the patient's position may have changed, or the set may have been incorrectly configured. A pressure-driven infusion also requires appropriate controls.
Q9. Why might a pump be preferred in a neonate?
A suitable infusion pump can deliver small volumes at a more accurately controlled rate than gravity infusion, which is important when the margin for fluid or medication error is narrow.
Q10. What observations would you document?
The fluid and volume prescribed, start time, delivery rate, relevant IV site findings, patient response and any complications or interventions.
Common mistakes that lose marks:
Failing to check the prescription or patient identity.
Touching the sterile spike or distal connector.
Forgetting to close the roller clamp before inserting the spike.
Overfilling or failing to fill the drip chamber adequately.
Connecting an unprimed line to the patient.
Failing to inspect the cannula site before starting.
Calculating the rate with hours instead of minutes.
Assuming all giving sets have the same drop factor.
Using an ordinary giving set when a special-purpose set is required.
Failing to monitor the patient after starting the infusion.
Examiner's tip: Verbalize both your action and its safety purpose. For example: “I am priming the tubing to expel air before connecting it to the patient, while maintaining asepsis.”
